prospect.name: Alex
prospect.location: Small town in central Florida, USA
prospect.occupation: Business owner since age 18. Runs a growing company with a team, KPIs and reporting, driving to job sites and walking properties; work is hybrid between office and field. Business email domain twqlc.com.
prospect.family_status: Second marriage, to a Colombian wife. Five children — three from his first marriage, plus a six-year-old and a 15-month-old daughter. Taking the call from a hospital waiting area where his daughter had been admitted for five days with ulcerative colitis.
prospect.training_background: Two-mile runs a few times a week, push-ups at home targeting about 50 a day, and a gym membership he uses maybe a couple of times a month. Has trained hard in one- to two-year stretches in the past and finds it comes back quickly after a lay-off. Spent a year vegan, trained consistently and got thin but built no muscle. Has never hired a personal trainer or any coach — "This is my first time ever approaching anybody for coaching or doing anything online." Has used kettlebells and other handled implements before.
prospect.medical: Left wrist injured in a snowboarding fall on ice about eight years ago and never medically assessed — "no I haven't done any medical." For roughly four years afterwards he could only do push-ups on his fists; it is now largely asymptomatic day to day but becomes tender if he trains it cold or without stretching. Separately, a prior shoulder injury from barbell work that took three to four months to settle. No other stiffness or limitation reported. Family, not the prospect: his youngest daughter has ulcerative colitis and was hospitalised during the call.

signals: Lost ground during a specific hard season — a newborn, a fast-growing company and a hospitalised child: "after having that baby kind of got comfortable I got comfortable you know so I'm just trying to looking to get back at it"

Wants a former self back, stated explicitly and with regret: "I remember when I was younger with my three other kids I had more energy to play with them and in my two kids now I play but it's not the same, it's not the same energy"

Not the_optimizer despite being a successful business owner — he is not currently fit (212 lb at 5'11", gym a couple of times a month) and price was a genuine barrier, not a quality signal: "it is a big commitment up front"
Buys like an operator though — "things that I've learned with my business is, you know, not to reinvent the wheel" — which is why the structure-and-accountability pitch landed cleanly

goals.text: Get lean and drop body fat, particularly the love handles
Build more muscle, especially upper body, while staying proportionate rather than big
Live as long as possible for his family and reach a point where the shape is easy to maintain as he ages
Have the energy to play with his 15-month-old and six-year-old the way he did with his first three children
Be a better father, employer and community leader by levelling himself up first
Training he can carry with him — RV trips, hotel gyms, weekends away with the kids
Keep up on family hiking, snowboarding, fishing and lobster-season trips
A proven, structured plan he can trust rather than assembling one himself

pains.text: No structured plan he believes in; loses motivation when the programme is self-assembled
Business schedule shifts constantly, so any rigid split routine collapses after a good two or three weeks
Years of trying to get in shape without the result sticking
Nutrition untracked — skips lunch, eats out at work, no macro awareness despite knowing the science
Got comfortable after the newborn arrived and stopped waking early to train
Left wrist still sensitive eight years after a snowboarding fracture-type injury that was never medically assessed
Noticeably less energy with his youngest two children than he had with his first three
Running is the only thing he sustains because it is portable, but it builds no strength or muscle
Daughter's ulcerative colitis and a five-day hospital admission consuming his attention during the decision

objections.raw_quote: $6,000, okay. Do you guys break it down monthly, or it has to be paid up front?
objections.rep_response: Gave the upfront norm — "most of the guys just put it on a credit card and handle it in one sitting. Why would you ask?" — then laid out three structures: pay in full, split in half at $3,000 with no interest, or six installments at $1,200 per month, which he described as carrying additional cost and totalling $7,200.

objections.raw_quote: let me um let me let me give me give me like 24 hours or 12 hours like to tomorrow to make a decision usually it is an investment i was maybe thinking it was going to be between five six hundred dollars a month kind of deal
objections.rep_response: Isolated properly — "Finances aside, like, there is, are you sure, like, there's nothing else keeping you from being 100%?" — probed for the real blocker with "what would be the reason that you wouldn't start right away" and "Is it that you're not sure how Trevor works with people and that gets you like in a hesitant state?", then ran the scripted belief question "do you actually feel that this can get you to your goals?" Resolved it not by playing OA through but by inventing a new commercial structure: a one-month $1,200 commitment with a decision point at thirty days.

objections.raw_quote: It's guaranteed I'm gonna do some of my research I just want to make sure I invest it right right I don't want to get hurt either and lose the money if there is a pause you know
objections.rep_response: Answered with the written strength guarantee and an injury-pause policy, and with a personal story about training on degenerated hips against a physician's advice. Did not run any of the scripted fear moves — notably not the burned-before move, despite the prospect volunteering exactly that story about employees he had trusted.

objections.raw_quote: I don't want to be the typical guy says I'm gonna talk to my wife right and let you get back
objections.rep_response: Compressed the play into one line — "you're a business owner you don't need to talk to your wife right" — and the prospect confirmed the decision was his: "ultimately that's not going to be it's my decision."

objections.raw_quote: And in the injuries, are they caused by the kettlebell workouts?
objections.rep_response: Attributed client injuries to the client rather than the modality — "someone not, how to say, you know, like just trying to be a bigger hero that they are" — and claimed "kettlebells are the least injury causing type of workout", contrasting with torn biceps and shoulders from bench pressing.

tiers.note: Stated offer — "the investment for the full transformation is $6,000 USD, and that's it."
Split in half: two payments of $3,000, explicitly no interest.
Off-menu: six monthly installments at $1,200/month, described as carrying additional cost. $1,200 above the stated price.
Off-menu, invented live to resolve the think-about-it objection: one month at $1,200, then a decision point on whether to continue.
Off-menu remainder if he continues after month one, which the rep said he thought could be split into two payments of $2,500. Agreed total if continued: $6,200.

offer.payment_plan_terms: Improvised on the call. $1,200 collected for month one as a trial with an explicit opt-out at thirty days; if he continues, $5,000 for the remaining five months, which the rep said "I think" could be split into two payments of $2,500. Total if continued: $6,200 — which matches neither the $6,000 upfront price nor the $7,200 six-installment price the rep had quoted ten minutes earlier.
offer.guarantee_mentioned: "It is in writing, you know, like, I don't think anybody in the fitness industry does that. What Trevor does is guaranteeing that in those six months, you will add eight kilos, which is around like 17 pounds, 17, 18 pounds, to your baseline weight of kettlebell that you start with, to all the basic movements. If you, if you wouldn't, for some reason, hit that, he will work for you until you do for free." Note: this guarantees strength progression, not the body-composition outcome the prospect came for.

prospect_financials.note: No financial-picture questions were asked. The only capacity signal is volunteered: "I could do the three thousand you know split it in half if it's no interest I'll probably do that route." His price expectation was $500-$1,000 per month.

Onboarding call with Trevor booked for 5:45pm the following day and a calendar confirmation sent.
Agreement email confirmed as received by the prospect, and a Skool community link included.

Counter-evidence: what closed is not the offer. He paid $1,200 for one month with an explicit right to walk at thirty days — "you're trying it out for a month and afterwards you decide" — so this is a one-month commitment, not a six-month sale.

Counter-evidence: the agreement was not signed on the call. The rep deferred it — "just remember to sign the agreement when you have time, somewhat in the afternoon today" — so nothing was executed live.
Counter-evidence: the terms he agreed to were invented during the call and are arithmetically inconsistent with both published structures.
outcome.next_step: Onboarding call with Trevor at 5:45pm on 1 July. Prospect to sign the agreement that afternoon, complete the onboarding questionnaire and join the Skool community before that call. Rep also opened a direct WhatsApp channel with him. Decision point on continuing at the end of month one.

notable.note: The best-run discovery in the batch and the most commercially irregular close. Phase 3 was excellent — five kids, the energy gap, kiteboarding, the reflect-back that got a clean "Correct." — and P11 was executed almost fully. But the consequence frame was skipped entirely for the third call in a row, and when the prospect asked for twelve to twenty-four hours the rep resolved it by inventing a one-month $1,200 trial with an opt-out and an improvised $5,000 remainder, producing a $6,200 total that matches no published price. Two further things a principal should see: the prospect disclosed an eight-year wrist injury he has never had medically assessed and was reassured about kettlebell press mechanics rather than screened; and the rep, asked about injury risk, told a story about being advised by his own physician to have both hips replaced at thirty, declining, and training with kettlebells instead. All of it happened while the prospect sat in a hospital where his daughter had been admitted for five days.
